items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let two compact smooth embedded surfaces span the same smooth link with supplied radial collars. Let $A$ be an isolated smooth radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior, with transverse boundary-curve crossings and equal ordered endpoint signs on the tori oriented outward toward the exterior.

There is a smooth ambient coordinate chart near $A$, with $A=[-1,1]\times\{0,0\}$, in which the first surface is $z=0$, $-1\le x\le1$, and the local link is the two end lines $x=\pm1,z=0$. An ambient topological isotopy supported in this chart, fixing that first surface and the literal link pointwise, carries the second surface in a smaller normal cylinder to
$$\{(x,R\cos\theta(x),R\sin\theta(x)):-1\le x\le1,\ |R|<r_0\},$$
where $\theta(x)=\pi(x+1)/2$ or $\pi(1-x)/2$. It fixes the common arc pointwise and introduces no other identifications. No differentiability of the ambient isotopy at the two end faces or at the common axis is asserted. This is a local surface-pair normal form, without a diagram reconstruction conclusion.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link $L$, with supplied radial collars in disjoint smooth normal tubes of $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily, orient the tube boundary tori by their outward normal toward the link exterior, and orient the two surface boundary curves compatibly with $L$. Let $\alpha$ be a smooth proper transverse common arc in the exterior, transverse to its boundary, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially to an isolated smooth embedded arc $A$ ending on $L$. Suppose its two ordered endpoint intersection signs agree, so their sum is $2$ or $-2$.

For every open neighborhood $U$ of $A$ there are a smooth closed ball $B\subset U$ with $A\subset\operatorname{int}B$ and a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $\operatorname{int}B$, such that its only non-singleton fiber is $A$, $q(B)=B$, and
$$(B,q((F_0\cup F_1)\cap B))\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\}).$$
Thus this actual local surface image is a properly embedded locally flat disk, including at the collapsed point. The surfaces may be disconnected or nonorientable. No definiteness or primeness assumption is needed for this local assertion.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a smooth link with chosen disjoint smooth normal tubes, and let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth embedded spanning surfaces with boundary $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily. Supply radial collar coordinates in the tubes in which each surface collar is given by a smooth ray direction depending on the boundary parameter. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and orient each torus of $\partial\nu L$ as the boundary of the oriented solid tube, so its outward normal points into $X$. Orient the two surface boundary curves on those tori compatibly with $L$.

Let $\alpha$ be a smoothly and properly embedded arc of transverse intersection of $F_0\cap X$ and $F_1\cap X$, transverse to $\partial X$, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially through the supplied collars to the corresponding points of $L$, obtaining a smooth embedded arc $A$. Assume a neighborhood of this extended arc contains no other intersection components. Write $i_0,i_1\in\{1,-1\}$ for the ordered local intersection signs of the two boundary curves at its endpoints, measured on $\partial\nu L$.

The union $F_0\cup F_1$ has a closed intrinsic neighborhood $K$ of $A$ modeled by four pages with common arc, glued at each end by one of the matchings $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$, with pages zero and two on $F_0$ and pages one and three on $F_1$. The two end matchings differ if and only if $i_0=i_1$. Consequently collapsing $A$ in this neighborhood gives a closed topological disk exactly when $i_0+i_1=2$ or $-2$. When $i_0+i_1=0$ it gives two disks joined at their interior centers. For the standard cases the ambient arc-collapse map can be chosen supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $A$, and its image of $K$ is an embedded topological disk. Local flatness of that disk is not asserted here.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] and shrink its fixed normal cylinder to $|x|\le1$, $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\le\delta$. Strict radius monotonicity and compactness give one point on each $F_1$ half at every sufficiently small normal radius $r>0$, for each $x\in[-1,1]$. They depend smoothly on $x,r$ for positive radius. The function $Z(x,t)$ is nonzero for $-1<x<1$ and $t\ne0$ in this cylinder, because otherwise there would be an extra intersection with $F_0$ away from $A$. Its linear coefficient $Z_t(x,0)$ is also nonzero there, by transversality along the open common arc. Reverse the $t$ coordinate if needed to make this coefficient positive. The two connected half-strips then have $Z>0$ for $t>0$ and $Z<0$ for $t<0$. Thus their positive-radius angles have unique lifts $\alpha_+(x,r)\in(0,\pi)$ and $\alpha_-(x,r)\in(\pi,2\pi)$ for interior $x$.

These lifts extend continuously to $r=0$ and the two end faces. Indeed $(Y,Z)=t\,v(x,t)$ with smooth nonzero $v$ on the closed strip; the normalized positive and negative half directions therefore extend uniformly as their signed $t$ tends to zero. At each end $v=(\sigma_\pm,0)$, so the positive-half angle is exactly zero or $\pi$, and the negative-half angle is respectively $\pi$ or $2\pi$. By [F2], $\sigma_-\ne\sigma_+$: the first surface has the same positive $y$ direction at its two boundary lines, so opposite end matchings mean precisely opposite signs for the second surface. Choose $\theta(x)=\pi(x+1)/2$ when $\sigma_-=1$, and $\theta(x)=\pi(1-x)/2$ otherwise. Its endpoint angles coincide with those of $\alpha_+$, and $\theta+\pi$ with those of $\alpha_-$.

Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\mu(r)$ equal to one near zero and zero near $\delta$. For $0\le u\le1$ and $-1<x<1$, prescribe target angles $\gamma_+=(1-u\mu)\alpha_++u\mu\theta$ and $\gamma_-=(1-u\mu)\alpha_-+u\mu(\theta+\pi)$. They remain respectively in $(0,\pi)$ and $(\pi,2\pi)$. On each normal circle use the increasing piecewise-affine angle map fixing $0,\pi,2\pi$ and taking $\alpha_\pm$ to $\gamma_\pm$, affine on each of the four intervening intervals. Its slopes are positive, so it and its inverse are circle homeomorphisms. The formulas depend continuously on $u,x,r$ as long as the breakpoints are distinct. At an end face they converge uniformly to the identity: the maximum angular displacement on the four affine intervals is bounded by $\max(|\gamma_+-\alpha_+|,|\gamma_--\alpha_-|)$, which tends to zero by step 2.1, uniformly in $r,u$. The inverses have the same uniform displacement bound. Define the angle maps to be the identity on the two end faces.

Preserve $x$ and normal radius and apply those angle maps for $r>0$; fix the axis at $r=0$. This gives a homeomorphism of the closed cylinder for each $u$, continuously in time, with the inverse furnished by the inverse angle maps. Continuity at the axis needs no angular limit: normal radius is unchanged. It is the identity at $u=0$, near the cylinder's radial boundary, and on both end faces by step 3.1, so it extends by the identity outside the cylinder to an ambient topological isotopy. It fixes the whole local first surface pointwise because the angles zero and $\pi$ are fixed, and fixes the local link on the end lines for the same reason. The chart was chosen to contain no other portions of the link or the first surface, so their remaining portions are fixed too.

At $u=1$ and $r$ so small that $\mu(r)=1$, the two $F_1$ half-strip angles are exactly $\theta(x)$ and $\theta(x)+\pi$. Their unique points at each normal radius thus fill exactly the signed-radius ruled strip in the Statement. The first surface remains its original flat strip and their boundary remains the literal two original end lines. Every map was an ambient homeomorphism fixing the axis, so no point identifications or extra intersections were introduced. This proves the relative local normal form, while retaining explicitly the topological regularity of the isotopy at its possible nonsmooth loci.

boundaries.reason: The input is one supplied isolated standard common arc with two distinct endpoints.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 fixes radius zero and proves continuity there from radius preservation, without an angular derivative or limit.
Step 5.1 reaches the ruled model at time one and treats a single arc; finite disjoint applications are separate uses.
Step 3.1 proves positive angular slopes while interior breakpoints are distinct, and separately proves uniform identity limits when breakpoints merge at either end face.
Step 2.1 identifies both endpoint angle lifts from the actual signed strip coordinates; Step 3.1 controls both inverse maps uniformly there.
The Statement assumes full AC inherited from the actual adapted-chart supplier; Step 3.1 uses explicit finite angular interpolation and a scalar cutoff only.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the actual adapted standard-arc chart supplier. Given that finite chart and its strip parameters, all angular interpolation maps and isotopy formulas are explicit and add no choice.

risk_review.notes: Isolation supplies angle half-plane signs on the whole smaller half-strip; no merely linear tangent estimate is substituted for actual intersections. The isotopy fixes the first surface and literal link, but is only topological at the axis/end faces. No crossing reconstruction yet.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Choose a proper strip around $A$ on $F_0$. Explicitly take a smooth transverse field along that interval, tangent to $L$ at its ends, extend it in finitely many surface charts tangent to the boundary, and use its short flow in [F1]. Normalize its restriction at each end to the unit boundary tangent, with whichever sign is continuous along the strip. Its flow coordinates give $c_0(x,y)$, $-1\le x\le1$, $|y|<\delta$, with $c_0(x,0)=A(x)$ and with the two end edges on $L$. Extend this map slightly across its end faces in the original smooth boundary charts, patching extensions off the prescribed strip if necessary. The strip is orientable, so its two tangent vectors define a smooth unit ambient normal. Its short normal exponential map gives a smooth ambient chart $(x,y,z)$ by [F1] and compact injectivity, with $F_0$ given by $z=0$, $-1\le x\le1$, and the two short pieces of $L$ by $x=\pm1,z=0$. The chart can be taken inside $U$, missing every other sheet of either embedded surface; locally these are the given surface charts, and compactness of the arc supplies a common sufficiently small width. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 On $F_1$ near $A$, the ambient coordinate $x$ is a submersion, since its derivative on $\dot A$ is one. Choose a nonzero smooth field in its one-dimensional kernel along $A$, and extend it nearby while retaining $dx=0$. One obtains this by subtracting the $x$ component with a local field having $dx=1$, then patching the kernel fields in finitely many charts, close enough to their fixed nonzero values along $A$. At the two end edges the kernel is exactly tangent to $L$, so choose its boundary value to be $\sigma_\pm\partial_y$, $\sigma_\pm\in\{1,-1\}$, with the sign continuous from the interior. Its flow from [F1] gives an actual parametrization $c_1(x,t)=(x,Y(x,t),Z(x,t))$, with $(Y,Z)(x,0)=0$ and with $Y(\pm1,t)=\sigma_\pm t$, $Z(\pm1,t)=0$. The two transverse derivatives $(Y_t,Z_t)$ are never simultaneously zero along the compact arc. The formula $v(x,t)=\int_0^1(Y_t,Z_t)(x,ut)\,du$ gives $(Y,Z)=t\,v(x,t)$ with smooth $v$ and $|v|>0$ on a uniform smaller strip. Thus its normal radius is $R(x,t)=|t|a(x,t)$ for smooth $a=|v|>0$, and shrinking makes $a+t a_t>0$ uniformly. It is strictly increasing on each positive transverse half and strictly decreasing on each negative half. [step 1.1, F1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Take the closed confocal ellipsoids $E_\rho=\{x^2/(1+\rho^2)+(y^2+z^2)/\rho^2\le1\}$ for $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$, choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small with strict margins inside the chart and the two strips. On either surface a point of $\partial E_\rho$ with axial coordinate $x\in[-1,1]$ has normal radius $R_\rho(x)=\rho\sqrt{1-x^2/(1+\rho^2)}>0$. By step 2.1, for each $x$ there is exactly one point of each transverse half of $F_1$ at this radius. For $F_0$ the two points are simply $y=\pm R_\rho(x),z=0$. Existence is uniform because $R_\rho\le\rho$ and the radii at the two fixed outer strip edges have a positive common lower bound. The implicit inverse in [F1] shows that these four edges, parametrized by $x\in[-1,1]$, depend smoothly on $x,\rho$ for $\rho>0$, including their endpoints; each is regular since its first coordinate is $x$. There are no surface points with $x$ beyond these end faces in this neighborhood: both surfaces have boundary exactly on those faces and point inward along $A$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, construct, algebra]

4.1 At $x=\pm1$ the radius is $\rho^2/\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$. Hence the four edge ends lie at the two points $y=\pm\rho^2/\sqrt{1+\rho^2},z=0$ on each end piece of $L$, with the same page pairings as in [F2]. Distinct pairings make their union $C_\rho$ one embedded circle. Its four corners have distinct tangent lines. Indeed boundary-curve transversality at the original arc endpoints says that the difference of the two radial angle functions has nonzero derivative there. For sufficiently small nonzero displacement along $L$, their angle difference is nonzero modulo $\pi$, so the two surface tangent planes at each of these corner points are distinct, meeting exactly in $TL$. Also $L$ is transverse to $\partial E_\rho$: its coordinate tangent is $\partial_y$ and the derivative of the ellipsoid equation in that direction is $2y/\rho^2\ne0$. If the two edge tangent lines on the ellipsoid agreed, that common line would lie in $TL\cap T\partial E_\rho=0$, a contradiction. This proves the required corner independence for every $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$ after shrinking once. The strict margins also permit a short extension past the outer radius. [step 3.1, F1, F2, construct, contradiction]

5.1 Use the actual confocal-ellipsoid collapse of [F3] in this adapted chart. It fixes $\partial E_\varepsilon$ and the outside, collapses exactly $A$, and sends $E_\rho$ to $(\rho/\varepsilon)E_\varepsilon$. On each positive level its restriction is the invertible linear map $(x,y,z)\mapsto(\rho\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\,x/(\varepsilon\sqrt{1+\rho^2}),y,z)$. Therefore it carries the four edges of $C_\rho$ to a regular four-edge circle with the same distinct corner tangent lines and smooth dependence on every positive $\rho$. Apply the fixed diagonal linear rescaling $E_\varepsilon\to B^3$ and put $r=\rho/\varepsilon$. These image circles are now exactly a finite-corner radial family satisfying [F4]; their cyclic edge ordering is fixed by the two end matchings and does not change with radius. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, construct, algebra]

6.1 Let $K=(F_0\cup F_1)\cap E_\varepsilon$. The level description in step 3.1 shows that it consists exactly of $A$ and the circles $C_\rho$, $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$. Thus after the collapse and diagonal rescaling its entire image, not just selected levels, is the radial disk in [F4]. That supplier gives a homeomorphism of the ball-disk pair to the standard pair. Pull back the diagonal rescaling to conclude that $(E_\varepsilon,q(K))$ is a standard ball-disk pair. Set $B$ to be this ellipsoid in the original ambient chart and extend the collapse by the identity outside it, as in [F3]. It is supported in $U$, has just $A$ as a nonsingleton fiber, and maps $B$ to itself. This proves the local flatness and all asserted support and fiber properties. Every construction used only the two local strips, so neither connectedness nor orientability of the complete surfaces was required. [step 3.1, step 5.1, F3, F4, construct] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual Proof 1.1–2.1 gives flat F0 and the x-preserving F1 strip with (Y,Z)=t v and monotone normal radius; the uniform smaller cylinder is derived locally.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Orient $\alpha$ from its first to its second endpoint, and extend this orientation to $A$. Along its open part choose continuous smooth transverse directions $u$ on $F_0$ and $v$ on $F_1$ so that the ordered triple $(\dot A,u,v)$ has positive ambient orientation. Such choices exist along an interval: choose the first direction in finite surface charts and interpolate consecutive signs consistently, and choose the sign of the second by the displayed orientation condition. Inside the radial collars these directions extend to nonzero boundary-tangent directions at the two points of $L$. To verify this, write the two collars as $(s,r,\theta_k(s))$. At a common radial arc their transverse tangents have base component $\partial_s$ and angular component $r\theta_k'(s)$ in the oriented unit angular direction of the normal disk. The boundary-curve transversality says $\theta_0'(s)-\theta_1'(s)\ne0$ there. Hence the orientation of their ordered transverse pair has constant nonzero sign for every $r>0$ and has a definite limiting sign choice on each copy of the boundary tangent at $r=0$. The individual directions remain transverse to $A$ on their own surfaces all the way to those endpoints. [given, construct]

2.1 These directions give relative strips on both surfaces. Extend the transverse field on each surface to a neighborhood of $A$, tangent to $L$ at its two ends, using finitely many surface charts and cutoffs. In the boundary charts take its restriction to $L$ to be a signed unit tangent for a common arclength parameter. Its short flow in [F1] sends $(t,r)$ to the time-$r$ point starting at $A(t)$; the two derivatives are independent on the zero section. By [F1], compactness and the same converging-collision argument as for a normal arc chart, it is an embedded rectangle for a sufficiently small uniform width. Uniqueness of the flow retains its two end edges on $L$. The positive and negative halves give two pages on each surface. By the isolated-intersection hypothesis, after shrinking they meet only along $A$ and their end edges on $L$. Their widths on these end edges can be chosen equal in the common arclength parameter, so the end identifications are pointwise in the page radius. Label the $u$-positive, $v$-positive, $u$-negative and $v$-negative pages by $0,1,2,3$. This gives exactly the asserted four-page neighborhood. [step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 At either exterior endpoint project $u,v$ to its boundary torus along $\dot A$. These are nonzero tangent vectors parallel respectively to the two boundary curves: each surface tangent plane contains $\dot A$ and its boundary-curve tangent. Let $s_0,s_1\in\{1,-1\}$ record whether those projected directions agree with the chosen orientations of the respective boundary curves. Following the radial collars to $L$ retains precisely these signs relative to the common oriented boundary tangent, by the collar coordinates in step 1.1. The positive page on $F_0$ is therefore glued to the positive page on $F_1$ exactly when $s_0s_1=1$. If the product is negative it is glued to the negative page instead. Thus the matching at that endpoint is $M$ for product $1$ and $N$ for product $-1$. This assertion uses the signs separately at each endpoint, not a presumed orientation of either whole surface. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 At the first endpoint $\dot A$ points from the solid tube into $X$; at the second it points back toward the solid tube. Projection along $\dot A$ consequently carries the oriented transverse plane determined by $(\dot A,u,v)$ to the oriented torus plane with sign $+1$ at the first endpoint and $-1$ at the second. Indeed the solid tube boundary orientation is defined by putting its outward normal first, and that normal has respectively positive and negative component along $\dot A$. Therefore the two local boundary intersection signs are $i_0=s_0^{\mathrm{first}}s_1^{\mathrm{first}}$ and $i_1=-s_0^{\mathrm{second}}s_1^{\mathrm{second}}$. By step 3.1 the end matchings differ exactly when the two products differ. These displayed formulas show this is equivalent to $i_0=i_1$. Equal matchings occur exactly when $i_0=-i_1$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Apply [F2] to the actual neighborhood in step 2.1. By step 4.1 the standard sign sums $2$ and $-2$ give its disk quotient, while sum zero gives the two-disk wedge. To realize the former quotient inside the ambient sphere use [F3] on the smooth arc $A$, with any prescribed neighborhood as support. Its restriction to the compact $K$ has exactly the same identifications as $K/A$. The induced map of that quotient onto its image in $S^3$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism. Its image is therefore an embedded topological disk. The construction has proved its intrinsic topology and its ambient embedding, while making no local-flatness conclusion at the collapsed point. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F2, F3, construct] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual page signs/matchings Proof 2.1–4.1 identifies opposite signed F1 end fields when the F0 y field is the same at both end lines.
